intro: For eleven units you have read other people's sacred texts: the Sabbath commandment in Exodus, the Sermon on the Mount, the opening sura of the Qur'an, Krishna's counsel to Arjuna, the Buddha's first teaching, the sayings of Confucius, the hymns of Guru Nanak, and stories told by elders of the Great Lakes and West Africa. In the last unit six students answered one question from six traditions. Now the question is yours. You will choose it, find the texts, and argue what three traditions would say.

This unit has two chapters. The first follows a student named Maya from a blank index card to a stack of quoted, cited and carefully read primary sources. You will learn to shrink a topic into a researchable question, to find reliable translations, to read with author, audience and purpose, to cite each scripture in its own system, and to avoid stereotype. The second chapter follows her to the front of the room, where she writes a thesis, builds layered evidence, compares without ranking, and answers questions from her classmates.

The capstone is not a test of what you believe. Students of every faith and of none do the same work on equal terms. It is a test of whether you can read what others hold sacred accurately and fairly, and report what you found in a way a thoughtful member of each tradition would recognize. By the end you will be able to pose a comparative question, gather and cite primary texts, and argue from them in writing and aloud.
bigQuestion: How can you let three traditions' own texts answer a question you care about, fairly, accurately and without ranking them?

timeline.t: The King James Bible is published in England
James Legge publishes his English Analects; J. M. Rodwell publishes his Qur'an
Max Müller's Sacred Books of the East series begins to appear
Edwin Arnold publishes The Song Celestial, a verse Bhagavad Gita
The World's Parliament of Religions meets in Chicago
Max Arthur Macauliffe publishes The Sikh Religion in six volumes
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its English Tanakh
The Bahá'í House of Worship in Wilmette is dedicated
Abington v. Schempp: the Supreme Court affirms objective study of religion in public schools
A centennial Parliament of the World's Religions returns to Chicago

words.d: a question that is open, that more than one tradition has addressed, and that can be answered from primary texts
the tradition's own text, story or ceremony, such as a verse of the Qur'an or a psalm
a scholar's or adherent's interpretation of a primary text, such as a commentary
works whose copyright has expired, so anyone may copy and quote them freely
the address of a passage, such as book, chapter and verse, plus the translation used
the kind of writing a text is, such as law, story, poetry, prophecy, letter or teaching
a community's long conversation about what its texts mean, carried in commentaries and teaching
stretching a claim beyond its evidence, as when one text or one person speaks for a whole tradition
the central claim of a paper, which the rest of the paper sets out to prove
the sentence of reasoning that explains why a piece of evidence supports a claim
naming whose belief or text a statement comes from, as in according to the Gita
a working knowledge of what the world's traditions teach and practice, and the ability to discuss them accurately

test.q: Which question is researchable for the capstone?
choices: What do the Torah, the Dhammapada and the Guru Granth Sahib say about forgiving an enemy, and why?
Which religion forgives best?
Do Buddhists forgive?
Is forgiveness good?
test.why: It is open, names three texts, asks for reasons and stays descriptive rather than ranking.

test.q: For a question about what the Gita teaches, which is a secondary source?
choices: Arnold's 1885 verse translation of the Gita
Ramanuja's commentary on the Gita
The Sanskrit text of chapter 2
An encyclopedia summary of Hinduism
test.why: A commentary interprets the primary text. The translation and Sanskrit are primary; the encyclopedia is tertiary.

test.q: What problem does Rodwell's 1861 Qur'an raise for citation?
choices: It has no verse numbers
It is still under copyright
He rearranged the suras, so his chapter numbers differ from the standard order
He translated from Persian
test.why: Rodwell reordered the suras into a guessed chronology, so a paper must cite the standard numbering.

test.q: How is the Guru Granth Sahib usually cited?
choices: By book, chapter and verse
By sura and ayah
By tractate and folio
By ang, the page of the standard edition, often with the composer
test.why: The standard edition has 1,430 angs, and hymns are often cited with the Guru or saint who composed them.

test.q: Before quoting Micah 6:8, a student notes it is a prophet speaking to people accused of cheating the poor. Which tool is she using?
choices: Author, audience and purpose
Tertiary sourcing
Point-by-point structure
Peer review
test.why: Asking who speaks, to whom and why is the author, audience and purpose toolkit from the first unit.

test.q: Exodus 20 grounds the Sabbath in creation. Deuteronomy 5 grounds it in what?
choices: The building of the Temple
The memory of slavery in Egypt
The covenant with Noah
The giving of the Talmud
test.why: Deuteronomy 5:15 tells the people to remember they were servants in Egypt, so their own servants must rest.

choices: All Muslims read the Qur'an the same way
Buddhists all meditate daily
Many Muslim scholars have read Qur'an 2:190 as permitting fighting in defense and within limits
Every Hindu reads the Gita as Gandhi did
test.why: It uses a qualifier, attributes the reading and names the verse; the others apply one idea to everyone.

choices: Sikh spoken exposition of scripture
A Confucian school of thought
A Hindu commentary on the Gita
The Islamic discipline of Qur'an commentary
test.why: Tafsir explains the Qur'an verse by verse. Katha is the Sikh term; Shankara and Ramanuja wrote Hindu commentaries.

choices: A careful reader could disagree, so evidence is needed to support it
It ranks one tradition above another
It states a fact no one disputes
It quotes a sacred text directly
test.why: An arguable thesis invites evidence. Ranking cannot be settled by any text, and an undisputed fact needs no argument.

test.q: What do Orthodox, Conservative and Reform Judaism illustrate in a capstone paper?
choices: Three different religions
Diversity within one tradition that a paper should name
Three schools of Confucian thought
Three translations of the Tanakh
test.why: They are branches of Judaism with different views of Jewish law, and a fair paper names the branch it means.

choices: The Torah sets a weekly day of rest
The Analects ask rulers to use labor at fitting seasons
Confucianism lacks a proper Sabbath
The Gita teaches moderation in sleep and waking
test.why: Saying Confucianism lacks a Sabbath measures it by Judaism's standard instead of describing it in its own terms.

test.q: Why is murti a better word than idol in a paper on Hindu practice?
choices: Murti is shorter
Idol is a Sanskrit word
Murti refers only to temples in India
Murti is the tradition's own term, while idol carries an outsider's judgment
test.why: A murti is a sacred image in which many Hindus understand the deity to be present; idol is a loaded word.

test.q: In an oral presentation, what should a speaker do when reading a sacred text aloud?
choices: Read it exactly as printed and name the translation
Summarize it loosely to save time
Change old words into slang
Skip the citation, since listeners cannot see it
test.why: Listeners should know whose words they are hearing, and a sacred text quoted wrongly is a text misrepresented.

test.q: A classmate asks Maya which view she personally agrees with. Which response fits the chapter's guidance?
choices: Rank the traditions from best to worst
Decline politely and point back to what each tradition would say
Refuse to answer any more questions
Say all three views are identical
test.why: The assignment asks what each tradition would say. A presenter may share a view if allowed, but must not rank.

test.q: Which statement about the 1963 Schempp decision is accurate?
choices: It required daily Bible reading in public schools
It banned any mention of religion in public schools
It ruled out devotional Bible reading while affirming objective study of religion
It was decided by the Illinois Supreme Court
test.why: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled out school-led devotional Bible reading, and Justice Clark's opinion affirmed objective study.

write.prompt: Choose a question about work, family, forgiveness, the natural world, wealth or war. Cite one primary text from each of three traditions studied in this course. Argue what each tradition would say and why, using the text, its context and how adherents read it, and end with a comparison that names both a parallel and a contrast.
tips: Name the text, its chapter and verse or its tradition's own citation system, and the translation every time you quote.
Attribute every belief: according to the Torah, many Buddhists hold, in Sikh teaching.
Name the branch or school you mean, and report at least one disagreement within a tradition.
Compare rather than judge: show where the answers meet and where they part, without ranking.
Use the unit's terms: thesis, warrant, genre, primary source, interpretive tradition.
